title: Sorry, Europe: Trump Has Found Better Allies in Asia
gist: Trump has binned US allies into two categories: Europe (Poland excepted) gets minimal diplomatic energy, while Japan, South Korea, the Philippines and Australia get close military coordination. The logic is a rejuvenated Monroe Doctrine plus China-first prioritization, with Russia downgraded to an irritant Europeans should handle themselves.

insights.claim: Trump has sorted US allies into those worthy of diplomatic energy and close military coordination and those who are not, with European nations - excepting Poland - placed in the 'not' category.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: A durable two-tier alliance model implies European defense procurement must assume less US involvement, while Asian allies retain access to US systems and coordination.
insights.quote: He has sorted the United States’s allies, by and large, into two categories: those worthy of diplomatic energy and close military coordination, and those who are not.
insights.locator: President Donald Trump is not a leader

insights.claim: Japan, South Korea, the Philippines and Australia are the four Asian allies receiving favorable treatment from Washington, described as the 'gung-ho Asian tigers' who get the green tick.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: These four are the most likely recipients of US technology transfer, co-production and basing investment - a concentration point for allied defense-industrial partnerships.
insights.quote: The gung-ho Asian tigers — Japan, South Korea, the Philippines, and Australia — get the green tick.
insights.locator: President Donald Trump is not a leader

insights.claim: Trump can afford to give European partners only a few days of summitry but cannot treat America's Asian allies the same way, implying US commitments in Asia are structurally more durable than in Europe.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Asymmetric credibility of US commitments argues for divergence between European and Asian defense-spending and security-risk pricing.
insights.quote: Trump may think his European partners are not worth more than a few days of summitry. He cannot think the same about the U.S.’s golden allies in Asia.
insights.locator: Trump may think his European partners

insights.claim: The alliance split is driven by geography: the Western Hemisphere is paramount under a rejuvenated Monroe Doctrine, and Asia - where peer competitor China sits - ranks well above Europe.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: A three-tier priority stack (hemisphere > Asia > Europe) is a usable filter for where US budget, forces and diplomatic capital will flow over the next several years.
insights.quote: While the Western Hemisphere is paramount under a rejuvenated Monroe Doctrine, Asia, where peer competitor China resides, is much more important than Europe.
insights.locator: The division is partly explained by geography

insights.claim: The stated end-goal is to concentrate US might on containing an increasingly hegemonic China, conditional on the Middle East not consuming American attention and resources.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: The Middle East is the explicit swing variable on the Asia pivot - a prolonged war there delays force and materiel flow to the Indo-Pacific.
insights.quote: This will allow the U.S., should the Middle East permit it, to focus its might on containing an increasingly hegemonic China.
insights.locator: The Ukraine-Russia war may be an irritant

insights.claim: Trump does not regard Putin's Russia as a major geopolitical threat and treats the Ukraine-Russia war as an irritant rather than a first-order strategic problem.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: If Russia is not treated as a first-order threat, US materiel and diplomatic support for Ukraine stays capped regardless of battlefield developments.
insights.quote: Trump doesn’t see Vladimir Putin’s Russia as a major geopolitical threat.
insights.locator: The Ukraine-Russia war may be an irritant

insights.claim: Washington wants Europeans to handle their own eastern border, shifting the burden of conventional deterrence against Russia onto European states.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Supports sustained multi-year European defense budget growth and demand for European-sourced land, air-defense and munitions capacity.
insights.quote: He wants the Europeans to handle their eastern border in any case.
insights.locator: The Ukraine-Russia war may be an irritant
